description: We are student innovators from SEDS Philippines, combining computing, electronics, aerospace, and physics to build LuNav. Franchesca Visitacion led backend and astronomical processing; Gian Nepomuceno designed the frontend; Chad Marera integrated NASA resources; Danica Bito-on researched Earth communication windows; Gianne Cirio defined rover power and survival constraints; and Miguel developed lunar terrain and horizon models. Together, we make lunar mission planning more accessible.
summary:
LuNav is an interactive web-based lunar mission-planning and visualization tool designed to simplify the assessment of solar illumination and Earth communication availability at potential lunar landing sites, particularly in the Moon's South Pole region. Its challenging terrain, low solar elevation angles, and prolonged shadows can significantly affect power generation and communication.

By combining NASA/JPL Horizons astronomical data with lunar terrain information, LuNav lets users explore landing locations and observation periods through intuitive visualizations. The tool estimates sunlight availability and solar power potential, evaluates terrain-aware visibility of the Sun and Earth, and models communication link conditions, including visibility to NASA ground stations.

LuNav addresses the difficulty of navigating multiple specialized scientific platforms by bringing key environmental and geometric assessments into one accessible interface. It supports more informed preliminary landing-site comparisons and mission planning for future robotic and human lunar exploration.
details:
Detailed Project Description (Link to GitHub: https://github.com/chescamargarette/LuNav)

  1. Project Overview

LuNav is an interactive web-based lunar surface environmental assessment and mission-planning tool built around two critical operational requirements for robotic landers and rovers: solar energy availability and communication with Earth. It primarily targets candidate landing sites in the Moon's south polar region, while also allowing users to explore historical lunar landing locations and compare environmental conditions across different mission dates.

Existing lunar exploration tools address parts of this task through different workflows. NASA Moon Trek and LROC QuickMap support lunar mapping and topographical assessment, while NASA/JPL Horizons provides high-precision astronomical position data. LuNav's novelty lies in bringing these scientific foundations together with preliminary power and communication models in a single, accessible environment.

The platform addresses two immediate mission-planning questions: when might sufficient sunlight be available to support solar-powered lunar operations, and when might a communication link with Earth be possible? By presenting the time-dependent positions of the Sun and Earth alongside terrain conditions, estimated power availability, and communication assessments, LuNav helps users recognize operational trade-offs without manually combining information from several specialized scientific platforms.

This preliminary screening is especially important in the Moon's south polar region. The Moon's axial tilt of approximately 1.54° causes the Sun to remain close to the polar horizon, producing prolonged shadows and regions that receive little or no direct sunlight. Similarly, Earth may appear close to the horizon or become obstructed by surrounding terrain, creating challenges for direct-to-Earth communication.

A location with favorable sunlight conditions may therefore not necessarily provide equally favorable communication opportunities. LuNav seeks to make these relationships easier to investigate and understand during the early stages of lunar mission planning.

  1. Core Functionalities

A. Sun and Earth Position Visualization

LuNav displays the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth relative to a selected lunar surface location. The application retrieves astronomical position data from NASA/JPL Horizons, including the elevation and azimuth angles of both celestial bodies over a user-defined observation period.

Users can specify lunar coordinates manually or select from predefined historical landing sites, including the Apollo missions, Chandrayaan-3, and Intuitive Machines lunar missions. They can also customize observation dates, times, time zones, and sampling intervals.

These inputs allow users to examine how the positions of the Sun and Earth change over time, identify potential sunrise and sunset periods, and recognize intervals when either celestial body may be obstructed by the lunar horizon.

The resulting information is presented through interactive visualizations and time-dependent analysis results, making astronomical geometry easier to interpret.

B. Solar Illumination and Power Assessment

LuNav evaluates preliminary solar illumination conditions at selected lunar locations by combining the calculated position of the Sun with the local horizon.

Where supported terrain data is available, the application considers terrain-generated obstruction to determine whether direct sunlight may reach the selected location. This helps identify potential illumination periods, prolonged darkness, and environmental conditions that may affect solar-powered lunar operations.

Beyond sunlight visibility, LuNav incorporates a simplified solar power and battery model. Using assumed solar irradiance, solar panel characteristics, power consumption, and battery specifications, the application estimates potential power generation and energy availability over the selected observation period.

These calculations help users examine the relationship between sunlight exposure, energy generation, and electrical storage requirements.

The resulting estimates are intended for preliminary engineering assessments rather than detailed spacecraft power-system validation. Actual performance would depend on the spacecraft's hardware configuration, panel orientation, thermal conditions, and operational power demands.

C. Earth Communication and Ground Station Visibility

LuNav evaluates potential direct-to-Earth communication opportunities by examining Earth's position relative to the local lunar horizon. By analyzing the elevation and azimuth of Earth, the application identifies periods when a direct communication path may be geometrically possible.

Where terrain information is available, the visibility assessment also considers potential obstructions from surrounding lunar topography.

The platform extends this assessment by incorporating simplified communication link-budget calculations. These models consider factors such as Earth–Moon distance, transmission frequency, free-space path loss, and assumed spacecraft communication parameters to estimate preliminary link conditions.

LuNav also includes modeled visibility assessments involving selected ground stations associated with NASA's Lunar Exploration Ground Sites (LEGS) initiative. This allows users to investigate how ground station geometry and the Earth's rotation influence potential communication opportunities between lunar surface assets and terrestrial receiving stations.

Together, these features support the identification of possible communication windows, potential signal limitations, and operational periods that may require alternative communication arrangements.

The calculations provide preliminary feasibility indicators and do not guarantee successful communication under actual mission conditions.

D. Landing Site and Mission Window Comparison

LuNav provides an environment for examining candidate lunar landing locations and observation periods based on their environmental and operational conditions.

Rather than assessing astronomical parameters independently, users can evaluate how changes in location and time influence sunlight availability, solar power potential, Earth visibility, communication link conditions, and other modeled constraints.

The platform includes site exploration and mission-window discovery features intended to help users identify potentially favorable locations and observation periods based on the available calculations and selected criteria.

By consolidating these assessments, LuNav supports preliminary comparisons of candidate landing sites and helps users recognize the trade-offs between power generation and communication availability.

E. Interactive Lunar Visualization

LuNav incorporates interactive lunar mapping and three-dimensional visualization to complement its numerical assessments.

Users can explore lunar locations, examine landing-site coordinates, and connect the calculated environmental conditions with their geographic context.

The combination of graphical representations, time-dependent analysis results, and mission-planning controls is intended to make complex lunar environmental information more understandable to researchers, students, and space exploration enthusiasts.

  1. Scientific and Computational Methodology

LuNav draws upon established astronomical and lunar surface datasets to support its scientific calculations. Its analysis combines astronomical geometry, terrain-based visibility assessment, and simplified engineering models for power and communication.

A. Astronomical Position Calculations

NASA/JPL Horizons serves as the primary reference for high-precision solar system ephemerides.

For each analysis, users specify a lunar surface location and observation period. LuNav retrieves observer-centered astronomical data describing the apparent positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the selected lunar coordinates.

These data include the elevation and azimuth angles used to determine geometric visibility. The application interprets these astronomical outputs instead of independently calculating planetary ephemerides.

Measurements at successive time steps form the basis for evaluating illumination conditions, visibility intervals, and changes in environmental conditions throughout the observation period.

B. Lunar Surface and Topographical Analysis

Lunar topography is particularly important near the poles, where even relatively small elevations can obstruct the low-angle Sun or Earth.

LuNav uses terrain information derived from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) aboard NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter to support its terrain-based assessments.

For locations covered by the processed terrain dataset, surrounding elevations can be represented through directional horizon profiles. These profiles are compared with the calculated positions of the Sun and Earth to estimate whether the line of sight is obstructed.

The analysis distinguishes between ideal geometric visibility and terrain-adjusted visibility where suitable terrain profiles are available. Locations without supported terrain coverage may rely on a simplified local-horizon assumption.

NASA Moon Trek and LROC QuickMap also provide mapping and scientific references for examining lunar surface features and understanding the geographical context of candidate landing areas.

C. Solar Power and Energy Modeling

The solar power assessment uses the estimated illumination conditions together with assumed engineering parameters.

These include incident solar irradiance, effective solar panel area, conversion efficiency, electrical load, and battery capacity. The model estimates potential energy generation and battery behavior over the selected observation period.

These calculations allow the influence of changing sunlight conditions to be examined through preliminary power availability estimates.

The model is intended to demonstrate the relationship between lunar illumination and energy-system performance, rather than to reproduce the full electrical and thermal behavior of a flight-qualified lunar spacecraft.

D. Communication Link Analysis

The communication assessment combines astronomical geometry with simplified radio-frequency propagation calculations.

Earth–Moon distance and the assumed communication frequency are used to estimate free-space path loss. Together with modeled transmitter power, antenna characteristics, and receiver sensitivity, these values support preliminary communication link-margin estimates.

The ground station analysis additionally considers the geometric visibility of selected terrestrial receiving stations and the time-dependent relationship between Earth and the lunar surface location.

These assessments help distinguish periods of potential geometric visibility from periods in which the assumed communication system may satisfy its modeled link requirements.

  1. Development Tools and Technologies

LuNav was developed as a browser-accessible web application using the following technologies and scientific resources:

Next.js, React, and TypeScript: Development of the interactive frontend, application logic, and server-side API endpoints.

Tailwind CSS: Interface styling and responsive dashboard design.

CesiumJS: Interactive three-dimensional lunar visualization.

NASA Moon Trek: Lunar mapping and geographical visualization resources.

NASA/JPL Horizons API: Astronomical ephemerides and observer-centered Sun and Earth position data.

NASA LOLA Data: Lunar terrain elevation information used for supported topographical and horizon analyses.

LROC QuickMap: Reference imagery and supporting lunar surface information.

Python: Preparation and processing of lunar terrain datasets and associated computational resources.

GitHub: Source-code management and collaborative development.

Vercel: Deployment and public hosting of the web application.

LuNav integrates its scientific calculations through web-based software, without requiring specialized physical hardware to operate. Users can access the deployed platform through a standard web browser.

  1. Expected Benefits and Project Goals

LuNav aims to reduce the complexity of preliminary lunar mission planning by making important astronomical, environmental, and engineering information easier to access and interpret.

Its primary benefit is the integration of several interconnected mission-planning considerations within a single platform. By combining sunlight visibility, solar power estimates, terrain conditions, Earth communication geometry, and modeled link performance, LuNav allows users to examine relationships that would otherwise require separate analyses.

The platform also makes specialized scientific information more accessible to students, educators, researchers, and the general public. Its visual approach demonstrates how celestial mechanics, lunar topography, electrical power systems, and communication engineering influence the feasibility of lunar surface operations.

For preliminary mission planning, LuNav can help identify potentially unfavorable illumination conditions, communication interruptions, and power-related constraints before more detailed investigations are conducted.

The project's intended impact is to promote accessible, data-informed lunar exploration planning while encouraging a broader understanding of the engineering challenges involved in future robotic and human lunar missions.

  1. Long-Term Vision

LuNav is intended to evolve into a more comprehensive preliminary decision-support platform that bridges the gap between early mission concepts and detailed engineering assessments for lunar surface exploration.

The current prototype establishes a foundation for integrating astronomical position data, terrain information, solar energy estimates, and communication feasibility models.

Future development may expand the coverage and resolution of terrain-based visibility assessments, improve the accuracy of solar panel and battery models, incorporate more detailed thermal and communication system parameters, and evaluate the availability of lunar relay satellites.

Additional validation against established scientific datasets and mission-specific engineering requirements would further improve the platform's reliability for practical mission-planning applications.

By consolidating these interconnected environmental, power, and communication variables within a single accessible environment, LuNav seeks to clarify the trade-offs involved in lunar surface operations. This integrated approach is intended to help engineers, researchers, and students identify critical mission constraints at an early stage, compare candidate exploration sites more effectively, and develop more informed mission timelines for future lunar exploration.
